results.description: Increase work-group size from 64 to 256 (nwarps=16 _INTEL macros)
results.build_config: GGML_SYCL_FORCE_MMQ (compile-time define to force MMQ dispatch)
results.notes: MMQ disabled by default (accuracy issues noted by original devs). Enabled for 7 types (QI<=16). Results show MMQ is slower than all alternative dispatch paths. Reverted ggml_sycl_supports_mmq to return false. mmq.cpp improvements kept dormant.

benchmark_comparison.summary: MMQ is 2.2x slower than MMVQ/DMMV for n<=8 and 1.6x slower than oneMKL for n=512. Standard build with dormant mmq.cpp changes shows no regression (ratio 1.00).

results.description: Increase MMVQ work-group size from 32 to 256 + new mul_mat_vec_q_multicol kernel for non-IQ types at n=2..8
results.notes: Two changes: (1) WG size 32->256 for all legacy MMVQ launchers, (2) new mul_mat_vec_q_multicol kernel for non-IQ quantized types when src1_ncols=2..8. IQ formats use old kernel templates with WG=256 (no multicol). The multicol kernel processes multiple output columns per work-group, dramatically improving efficiency for speculative decoding batch sizes.

n1_wg256_only.description: n=1: WG size increase only, no multicol

n2_8_non_iq_multicol.description: n=2..8: non-IQ types using multicol kernel

n2_8_iq_fallback.description: n=2..8: IQ types using legacy kernel with WG=256

observations: q4_K and q5_K show lower multicol speedups (1.3-1.8x) vs other non-IQ types (2-7x) - likely due to larger block sizes reducing parallelism benefit
IQ types show no benefit from WG=256 change alone; multicol kernel needed but requires IQ dequant support
Speedup scales strongly with n for multicol types: n=2 ~2x, n=5 ~3-4x, n=8 ~5-7x
q6_K and q8_0 show the largest speedups at n=8 (7.5x, 7.1x) likely due to highest memory bandwidth savings from column batching

results.description: Replace dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor butterfly reduction with sycl::reduce_over_group in all 11 legacy/multicol/reorder MMVQ kernels
results.notes: Replaced all 11 instances of manual butterfly shuffle reduction (dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor loop) with native sycl::reduce_over_group(sub_group, tmp, sycl::plus<float>()). Also updated leader-thread check from get_local_id(2)==0 to get_sub_group().get_local_linear_id()==0. Build succeeded, correctness passed (730/730), but benchmarks showed net regression. REVERTED.

overall.description: All quantized types across all n values — net 2.9% regression

observations: sycl::reduce_over_group has higher latency than manual butterfly shuffle for most sub-group configurations on Xe2
Severe regressions concentrated at n=2 and n=3 for multicol types — possibly related to sub-group reduction implementation overhead
A few types (iq2_xxs, iq4_xs, q4_K, q5_K) showed improvements but not enough to offset widespread regressions
The Xe2 compiler/runtime appears to generate worse code for reduce_over_group than hand-rolled butterfly xor shuffles
Changes reverted; dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor remains the preferred reduction pattern on this hardware

results.description: Vectorized 64-bit loads (get_int2_from_*) for q4_0, q4_1, q5_0, q5_1, q8_0 — replace per-element int32 loads with coalesced int64 loads
results.notes: Replaced loop-based 32-bit loads with widened 64-bit load helpers (get_int2_from_int8_aligned, get_int2_from_uint8_aligned, get_int2_from_int8, get_int2_from_uint8) in 5 non-K formats (q4_0, q4_1, q5_0, q5_1, q8_0), both legacy and reorder paths. Also simplified get_int_from_int8/uint8 to use __builtin_memcpy. For q5_0/q5_1, optimized qh loads to single load + two shifts. Build succeeded, correctness passed (730/730), but benchmarks showed net regression. REVERTED.

modified_5_formats_n1.description: Modified formats at n=1 — neutral (DMMV path, not MMVQ multicol)

overall_10_formats.description: All 10 non-IQ quantized types across all n values — net 4.0% regression

worst_regressions.note: ~21.6% regression despite some improvements at smaller n
~15.3% regression in unmodified format — possible cache pressure effect

observations: 64-bit loads do not reduce total instruction count enough to offset increased register pressure on Xe2
q4_0 and q5_0 are worst affected (15-25% regressions at n>=4), likely because their original 32-bit load loop was well-optimized by the compiler
q8_0 shows mixed results — improves at n=2,4,5 but regresses badly at n=8, suggesting it benefits from coalescing at smaller batch sizes but hits register spill at n=8
n=1 is neutral across all formats because it uses the DMMV path, not the MMVQ multicol kernel
Unmodified K-quants confirm changes are isolated; q6_K n=8 anomaly (-15.3%) may be noise or shared cache pressure
The Xe2 compiler appears to handle small unrolled loops (2 iterations) efficiently enough that manual vectorization adds overhead
Changes reverted; original loop-based 32-bit loads with #pragma unroll remain the better approach on this hardware

results.description: Cache Y vector in SLM (Shared Local Memory) to eliminate redundant global memory reads across sub-groups
results.build_config: Standard build with SLM caching via use_slm template parameter and MMVQ_SLM_Y_LIMIT=49152
results.notes: Implemented cooperative SLM load of Y vector (block_q8_1 blocks) in mul_mat_vec_q_multicol kernel. All 11 multicol launchers updated with slm_ok budget check and dual-path dispatch (use_slm=true/false). A/B benchmarked by toggling MMVQ_SLM_Y_LIMIT between 49152 (ON) and 0 (OFF).

summary.n2_n3_note: Mixed results: some types 10-43% faster with SLM OFF, others 10-14% slower. Not consistently beneficial.

benchmark_comparison.conclusion: SLM caching has no measurable benefit at n>=4 (<1.4% diff, within noise). At n=2,3 effects are mixed and inconsistent across types. Xe2 L1 cache handles Y-vector access efficiently without explicit SLM management. Code reverted for simplicity.

results.description: Add #pragma unroll to dequantization inner loops — Q4_K data-loading loops in vecdotq.hpp
results.notes: Added #pragma unroll to the only 2 loops missing it in the MMVQ path: vec_dot_q4_K_q8_1_common() and reorder_vec_dot_q_sycl<Q4_K>::operator() data-loading loops (QR4_K=2 iterations). All other loops in mmvq.cpp and vecdotq.hpp (IQ format loops, K-quant loops, reduction loops, reorder loops) already had #pragma unroll. Build succeeded, correctness passed (730/730), but benchmark showed 0% measurable improvement — Q4_K times within noise of opt_002_001 results. The compiler already unrolled these trivial 2-iteration loops. Code reverted.

benchmark_comparison.conclusion: All values within <1% of opt_002_001 results. No measurable impact from #pragma unroll on 2-iteration data-loading loops — compiler already unrolls them.

results.description: Standardize WG sizes to 256 for all dequant formats — multi-block-per-WG transformation for K-quant (q2_K, q3_K, q4_K, q5_K, q6_K), IQ (iq1_s, iq1_m, iq2_xxs, iq2_xs, iq2_s, iq3_xxs, iq3_s, iq4_xs, iq4_nl), and mxfp4 kernels
results.notes: Implemented multi-block-per-WG transformation: WG=64→256 kernels (q2_K, q3_K, q5_K, q6_K) process 4 quant blocks per WG; WG=32→256 kernels (q4_K, IQ formats, mxfp4) process 8 quant blocks per WG. Each kernel uses virtual sub-group indexing (sub_block = tid/orig_wg_size, tid = tid%orig_wg_size) with nb bounds checking. q4_K SLM expanded from 12 to 96 bytes (8 sub-blocks × 12). All 15 kernel bodies modified in dequantize.hpp, all launch configs updated in convert.cpp. Dequantize kernels cannot be benchmarked in isolation — no dedicated CONVERT test in test-backend-ops. Tested via MUL_MAT n=512 (GEMM fallback: dequantize + oneMKL) and MUL_MAT n=1 for IQ types. Dequantize is a tiny fraction of total MUL_MAT time, so improvements are invisible. REVERTED.

benchmark_comparison.test_case_1: MUL_MAT(type_a=*,type_b=f32,m=4096,n=512,k=14336) — K-quant and IQ types via GEMM fallback
benchmark_comparison.test_case_2: MUL_MAT(type_a=iq*,type_b=f32,m=4096,n=1,k=14336) — IQ types via GEMM fallback at n=1

mul_mat_n1_iq.description: IQ types at n=1 (GEMM fallback, dequantize + oneMKL)

benchmark_comparison.conclusion: No measurable speedup. Dequantize kernels are a tiny fraction of MUL_MAT execution time (dominated by oneMKL GEMM at n=512). WG=256 multi-block approach adds bounds-checking overhead without visible benefit. The K-quant/IQ dequantize kernels are already fast enough relative to downstream consumers. Remaining opt_task_008 steps (vectorization, nd_range cleanup, loop unroll, SLM caching) unlikely to show measurable improvement for the same reason — dequantize is not the bottleneck. Task abandoned.

results.description: Increase work-group size from 128 to 256 for better EU occupancy on Xe2
results.notes: Single-line change: block_size 128→256 in launch_bin_bcast(). Affects all binary broadcast operations (ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV, REPEAT) since they share the same launch function. The 3D grid partitioning (bx*by*bz) automatically adapts to the new block_size. For the broadcast test case (ne0=4096, nr=[1,512,1,1]), dimension collapsing merges ne0*ne1 into a single dimension, making this effectively a 1D launch with WG=256 processing 2M elements. Bandwidth improved from ~155 GB/s to ~328 GB/s (72% of B60 peak 456 GB/s).

results.description: Compile-time ncols specialization with #pragma unroll + dynamic block_size + compile-time block_reduce
results.notes: Added ncols_template and block_size_template template parameters to soft_max_f32_sycl kernel. 8 compile-time specializations matching CUDA: {32,64,128,256,512,1024,2048,4096}. Block sizes capped at WARP_SIZE*WARP_SIZE=256 (Xe2 block_reduce limitation: single warp reduces inter-warp partials, max WARP_SIZE warps). Specializations enable #pragma unroll on 3 inner loops and eliminate bounds checks when ncols_template>0. block_reduce gets compile-time block_size_const instead of 0 (runtime). New soft_max_dispatch_sycl helper routes to specialization or fallback. Initial attempt with block_size=1024 for ncols>=512 caused block_reduce corruption (40 test failures at ncols=1024); fixed by capping at 256.

overall.description: 1.77x average speedup across all 29 cases. Specialized paths average 2.99x. Peak bandwidth 365 GB/s (80% of B60 456 GB/s peak). Only 1 of 29 cases shows minor regression (4%, within noise).

results.description: Replace full-precision sycl::pow/sin/cos with sycl::native:: variants (exp2, cos, sin, log)
results.notes: Four changes in rope.cpp: (1) Precompute theta_scale_log2 = sycl::log2(theta_scale) on host, (2) Replace sycl::pow(theta_scale, X) with sycl::native::exp2(theta_scale_log2 * X) in all 4 kernel variants (norm, neox, multi, vision), (3) Replace sycl::cos/sin with sycl::native::cos/sin in rope_yarn, (4) Replace sycl::log with sycl::native::log in rope_yarn ext_factor path. Native math trades ~1 ULP accuracy for 3-5x faster transcendentals — acceptable for positional encoding where small errors are absorbed by attention softmax.

results.description: Reduce GROUP_NORM from 3 passes to 2 passes using float2 sum+sum_sq simultaneous accumulation
results.correctness: pass (51/51 norm tests: GROUP_NORM 2/2, RMS_NORM 17/17, NORM 16/16, L2_NORM 16/16)
results.notes: Replaced 3-pass GROUP_NORM (pass1: sum+reduce for mean, pass2: subtract_mean+write+sum_sq+reduce for variance, pass3: scale*read+write) with 2-pass approach using sycl::float2 accumulation: pass1 accumulates sum and sum-of-squares simultaneously (Var = E[x²]-E[x]²), pass2 writes (x-mean)*scale. Eliminates one full read+write pass over the data. Same approach already used by NORM kernel in this file. Also an improvement over CUDA GROUP_NORM which still uses 3 passes. SLM type changed from sycl::local_accessor<float> to sycl::local_accessor<sycl::float2> to support the float2 block_reduce.

data.note: Small case: 40960 elements/group, 160 iterations/thread — reduction overhead is non-trivial relative to data passes
Large case: 327680 elements/group, 1280 iterations/thread — eliminating the third pass saves ~425us of memory traffic

overall.description: 1.49x average speedup across both GROUP_NORM test cases by reducing 3 passes to 2. Large case improved from 62 to 92 GB/s. Bandwidth still well below peak (50.8%) due to GROUP_NORM's non-contiguous access pattern (groups span multiple channels) and high iteration count per thread.

results.description: Selective #pragma unroll 4 on hot inner loops in CONV_2D (c_in, ky, kx loops) and CONV_TRANSPOSE_1D (c, i loops). CONV_2D_DW and CONV_TRANSPOSE_2D left unmodified (unroll regressed those kernels).
results.notes: Added 5 #pragma unroll 4 directives total: 3 in conv2d kernel (c_in at line 134, ky at line 142, kx at line 147) and 2 in conv_transpose_1d kernel (c at line 50, i at line 57). Initial attempt with unroll on all 5 kernels showed CONV_2D_DW 0.93-0.96x regression and CONV_TRANSPOSE_2D 0.94-0.96x regression, so pragmas were removed from those two. CONV_2D high-channel cases show 1.16-1.22x speedup. CONV_2D low-channel cases (1-4 channels) show 0.68-0.89x regression due to unroll overhead with too-few loop iterations. Time-weighted net CONV_2D speedup ~1.05x (large workloads dominate). CONV_TRANSPOSE_1D shows clean 1.23-1.24x speedup.

results.description: Fix ~20% regression on ADD/SUB/MUL/DIV by reverting binbcast.cpp and binbcast.hpp to baseline
results.notes: binbcast kernel had ~20% regressions on ADD/SUB/MUL/DIV with ne=[4096,1,1,1], nr=[1,512,1,1]. Multiple optimization attempts failed: (1) enum dispatch to eliminate runtime op switch, (2) function pointer template approach, (3) surgical fixes targeting 64-bit casts, (4) block_size differences. None resolved the regression. Root cause was cumulative changes from prior optimization passes (opt_task_009 WG 128->256 was beneficial, but subsequent modifications introduced the regression). The only viable solution was reverting binbcast.cpp and binbcast.hpp to their baseline (pre-optimization) state, which restored original performance.

data.note: DIV slightly slower than baseline (60.45 vs 58.76) but regression eliminated (was 70.56)

summary.resolution: Full revert of binbcast.cpp and binbcast.hpp to baseline
investigation_attempts: Enum dispatch to eliminate runtime op switch — no improvement
Function pointer template approach — no improvement
Surgical fixes targeting 64-bit casts — no improvement
summary.description: All four ops restored to baseline performance after revert. ADD/SUB/MUL within 0.1% of baseline. DIV within 2.9% of baseline (60.45 vs 58.76 us). The prior WG 128->256 optimization from opt_task_009 is also lost, but the regression fix takes priority.

results.description: Fix ADD_ID regression by replacing hardcoded WG size 768 with hardware max_work_group_size (1024 on B60 dGPU)
results.notes: ADD_ID kernel used hardcoded 768 for max threads per work-group (from pre-upstream-fix code), while the baseline used ggml_sycl_info().max_work_group_sizes[ctx.device] which is 1024 on B60. For ne00=2880 with n_token=1, having 1024 threads vs 768 means each thread processes fewer elements (3 vs 4) and better sub-group occupancy. Fix: changed hardcoded 768 to hardware max_work_group_size query.
